oneSentence: Data leakage happens when future, target or held-out test information improperly influences model training or evaluation, making performance look better than it is.
plainExplanation:
A model learns from input data and then produces an output, such as a class label or a score. Leakage happens when model building uses information that would not exist in real use, or information that should have been reserved for a fair test. It also happens when evaluation cases overlap with training cases.

What goes in matters. If a spreadsheet includes a column created after the outcome happened, or if the same case appears in both training and test sets, the model can pick up shortcuts. Evaluation scores, such as accuracy, may then look unusually strong. The result is a misleading impression of quality.

A common form is target leakage. This means an input contains target-derived or later information that would not be available when the prediction is made. For example, predicting whether a document will be archived while including a field filled in only after archiving creates an unfair clue.

This is not the same as overfitting. Overfitting means a model matches quirks in the training data and then performs poorly on new data, even without leaked information. Leakage is a pipeline or evaluation flaw, so the score may be high for the wrong reason. A leaked model can seem excellent until it meets real-world data.

everydayAnalogy.title: A filing test with answer marks already showing
everydayAnalogy.story: A team is testing whether a new search assistant can sort policy documents into the right folders. One staff member quietly leaves coloured stickers on several folders that match the correct destination, because those stickers were added after the documents had already been filed. During the test, the assistant appears highly accurate because it follows the stickers rather than reading the documents carefully. When new unstickered documents arrive, its performance drops sharply.

mapping.aiElement: information created after the outcome that leaks the correct answer

mapping.analogyElement: assistant using stickers to sort folders
mapping.aiElement: model relying on leaked features instead of genuine patterns

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A search assistant in this story can visibly choose the stickers, while a machine learning model does not recognise leakage as suspicious. It only detects statistical patterns. Also, real leakage is often subtle, such as duplicated records, badly timed data preparation, or target-derived variables, not obvious marks placed on folders.

visual.title: Clean evaluation versus leaked evaluation
visual.learningObjective: After viewing, the reader should be able to explain why a high score can be misleading when future or target-related information enters training or testing.
visual.description: A side-by-side diagram with two lanes read left to right. The left lane shows a clean pipeline from raw features to split to train to test to realistic score. The right lane shows a leaked clue entering before training or testing, leading to an inflated score and poor real-world performance. A warning icon marks the leak point.

steps.label: Clean features
steps.explanation: Inputs contain only information that would be available when the prediction is actually made.
steps.visualInstruction: Left lane: draw a table labelled 'features available at prediction time' with neutral rows and columns.

steps.label: Proper split
steps.explanation: Training data and test data are kept separate so the test remains a fair check.
steps.visualInstruction: Left lane: split the table into two non-overlapping blocks labelled 'train' and 'test'.

steps.label: Realistic score
steps.explanation: The model is trained on train data and evaluated on test data, producing a score that is more likely to match real use.
steps.visualInstruction: Left lane: arrows from train to model, then from test to score card labelled 'credible evaluation'.

steps.label: Leaked clue enters
steps.explanation: A target-related field, future information, or duplicate case slips into the pipeline.
steps.visualInstruction: Right lane: show an extra highlighted column or duplicate row entering before the split, with a warning symbol.

steps.label: Inflated test result
steps.explanation: Because the model or the test has seen an unfair clue, the score looks better than true performance.
steps.visualInstruction: Right lane: arrows to a score card labelled 'too good to trust' with a higher number than the left lane.

steps.label: Deployment gap
steps.explanation: When the leaked clue is absent in real use, performance drops.
steps.visualInstruction: Right lane: final arrow to a box labelled 'real-world data without leaked clue' and a lower score badge.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each lane to highlight the causal path from input design to evaluation result; a toggle can reveal examples of 'future data', 'target-derived column', and 'train-test overlap'.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram compares two evaluation pipelines. In the clean pipeline, the input table contains only features available at prediction time. The data is split into separate training and test sets. A model trains on the training set and is scored on the test set, giving a credible result. In the leaked pipeline, an unfair clue enters before or during evaluation, such as future information, a column derived from the target, or duplicated cases across train and test. The model then gets an inflated score. When used on real-world data where that clue is absent, performance falls. The main message is that leakage creates misleadingly good evaluation results.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static two-column comparison replaces animation. The left column shows clean features, proper train-test separation, and a credible score. The right column shows a leaked clue entering, an inflated score, and then lower real-world performance when the clue disappears.

workedExample.scenario: A team wants to predict whether incoming grant emails need urgent follow-up within 24 hours.
workedExample.input: Training table with 10,000 past emails. Features include sender domain, subject words, language, and a field called 'follow_up_completed_time'.
process: The team trains a classifier and includes 'follow_up_completed_time' as an input feature.
On the test set, the model reaches 97% accuracy, much higher than the team's baseline of 78%.
A reviewer notices that 'follow_up_completed_time' is only filled after staff have already handled the urgent cases, so it indirectly reveals the outcome.
The team removes that field and re-runs the evaluation with a clean train-test split.
Accuracy falls to 81%, which is lower than 97% but much more believable for real incoming emails.
workedExample.result: The first score was inflated by target leakage. The cleaned model is less impressive on paper, but its test result is more likely to match real operations.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A country office wants to triage a shared programme inbox by predicting which messages need same-day response. The team uses approved internal tools and historical message metadata to test a model.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Leakage can appear if the dataset includes fields added after staff review, such as priority tags, escalation status, or closure times. That would make the pilot seem stronger than it would be on new incoming messages.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not upload confidential, personal, protection-sensitive, security-sensitive or operational email content or metadata to an unapproved AI service. Use approved environments, minimise data, and keep human oversight over triage decisions.

whyItMatters: A leaked model can pass testing, win budget, and enter operations even though it does not truly work. That creates poor decisions: systems may be procured, deployed or trusted on the basis of scores that were never a fair test. For programme teams, this can mean missed cases, wasted staff time, unfair treatment, or false confidence in dashboards and automation. For technical teams, leakage blocks honest comparison between models because the evaluation no longer reflects reality. Spotting leakage early helps teams ask a simple but powerful question: would this information really be available at the moment we need the prediction?

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If the test score is high, leakage cannot be the problem.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Leakage often creates exactly that pattern: unusually high scores that look impressive. A test set is only useful if it stays independent and realistic. If future information, duplicate cases, or target-derived fields slip in, the score stops being a trustworthy check.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Leakage only means someone intentionally copied answers into the dataset.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Most leakage is accidental. It can come from a harmless-looking preprocessing step, a timestamp mistake, a column updated after the outcome, or records from the same case appearing in both train and test. The issue is not intent; it is whether unfair information entered the pipeline.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Leakage and overfitting are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They can both lead to poor real-world performance, but the mechanism differs. Overfitting means the model learned noise or quirks in the training data. Leakage means the model or the evaluation had access to information it should not have had, so the score was contaminated from the start.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: A system can look smart in testing if it was given clues that would not exist in real use. Then the score is misleading.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Data leakage occurs when prediction-time-unavailable information or held-out evaluation information improperly influences model building, or when evaluation cases are not independent of training. Common mechanisms include target leakage, future data, duplicate or related records across splits, and preprocessing fitted on the full dataset before splitting. Leakage often makes evaluation overly optimistic because features, transformations or model choices benefit from information outside a fair pipeline. Memorisation is a model repeating training examples and can worsen duplicate-record leakage, but it is not the leakage itself. Data exfiltration is unauthorised copying out of a system, not this evaluation flaw. Check whether every feature existed at the prediction point and whether evaluation cases remained isolated from training and model selection.

keyTakeaway: If a model gets hidden clues during training or testing, a strong score may measure the leak, not the model.

quickCheck.question: Which situation is the clearest example of data leakage?
options: A model for same-day response uses message subject, sender, and language available when the message arrives.
A model is trained on last year's cases, but one useful feature is removed because it is noisy.
A model predicting hospital discharge risk uses a field completed after discharge decisions were made.
A model performs worse on a new region because writing styles differ from the training data.
quickCheck.explanation: The discharge-related field is created after the outcome process, so it carries future or target-related information that would not be available at prediction time. The other options describe normal feature choice or a generalisation problem, not leakage.

issues.problem: The definition is too narrow. Train-test contamination and preprocessing fitted on the full dataset can leak held-out evaluation information even when the underlying feature values would be available at prediction time. This also conflicts with mechanisms listed later on the page.
issues.fix: Data leakage happens when future, target or held-out test information improperly influences model training or evaluation, making performance look better than it is.

issues.problem: The target leakage definition says the input is merely "too closely tied" to the target. A strongly correlated feature is not leakage if it is legitimately available at prediction time. The problem is that the feature contains target-derived or later information that should not be available then.

issues.problem: Calling any "inappropriate or unrealistically correlated" information leakage is overbroad. An unstable proxy or spurious correlation can cause poor generalisation without any information crossing a training, time or evaluation boundary. The claim that leakage always "biases evaluation upward" is also too absolute. It commonly makes results optimistic, but the core defect is that the estimate is contaminated.

issues.problem: The page distinguishes leakage from overfitting but not from memorisation or data exfiltration, despite claiming separate entries for both. Duplicate-record leakage can enable memorisation, but leakage is the pipeline flaw while memorisation is model behaviour. Data exfiltration is unauthorised copying out of a system, not evaluation contamination.
